text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- The grumblers in east and west are talking again. Parliamentary speaker Rita suessmuth says that central problem is a mental one at Unity Day celebrations
- Compromise over local government's old debts is reached
- Post minister Wolfgang Boetsch approves raising the cost of sending mail despite resistance from Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt
- Row continues over sick pay cuts
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- German government plans tougher penalties for sex offenders and paedophiles

- President Bundesrat upper house of parliament Edmund Stoiber hails Hungarian Prime Minister Gyula Horn for "cutting the Iron Curtain" and helping unification at Unity Day celebrations in Munich and Berlin
- Deutsche Bank cuts sick pay for employees
- Post Minister Wolfgang Boetsch wants higher mail tarifs
HANDELSBLATT
- Business leaders hail Christian Democrats' tax plans but say a net reduction in tax burden of between 20 and 30 billion marks is too low
- Solution is found for old debts of local governments across Germany. The federal government agreed to take over 8.4 billion marks in old debts
- Hungarian Prime Minister Gyula Horn hails Germany's role in Europe at Unity Day celebrations in Germany
- Oscar Lafontaine, opposition Social Democrat leader, warned against overburdening public finances in the face of rising cost of civil servants' pensions
DIE WELT
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl (in Dublin) thanks Europe for unification. Politicians at Unity Day celebrations in Germany urge Germans from east and west to respect each other more
- Agreement after row over old debts in east Germany
- OeTV public sector workers' union keeps to 35-hour week. Union leader Herbert Mai says salaries may not necessarily be cut if work hours are cut
- Criticism of Christian Democrats' tax plans. DGB demands end to proposals to tax unemployment benefit and pensions
- Two men suspected of spying on Volkswagen believed to have been released
- Half of shops in Germany would take advantage of longer opening hours from November 1
